source_reviews.independent_solution: A wavefront is a surface whose points have the same phase at a fixed instant. A plane wave has parallel planar wavefronts. For phase k dot r - omega*t, fixing phase produces planes normal to k. A spherical wave has concentric spherical wavefronts; phase depending on radial distance produces constant-radius surfaces. In the usual homogeneous isotropic medium, outward spherical propagation is radial and plane-wave rays are parallel. The names classify wavefront geometry, not the direction of particle displacement: a wave is not plane merely because particles vibrate longitudinally, nor spherical merely because particles move along a radius. Finite sources provide these idealizations only in suitable regions.

source_reviews.independent_solution: The question explicitly concerns usual bulk elastic shear sound in ordinary gases and liquids, not liquid surface waves. Such propagation needs a restoring shear stress. In the ordinary fluid elastic model, the static shear modulus G is zero: shear displacement relaxes rather than producing a solid-like elastic restoring force. The elastic shear-wave relation v_s^2=G/rho therefore supplies no nonzero bulk elastic shear propagation speed. Compression still has a restoring pressure response, so longitudinal sound is allowed. Viscosity can cause shear perturbations to decay or diffuse, but does not turn them into the usual solid-like bulk elastic shear mode. Gravity and surface tension can restore surface displacements; surface-wave motion can mix vertical and horizontal components. That excluded surface phenomenon is not evidence of a pure bulk elastic shear wave.

coverage.evidence: Carry the frozen ordinary-fluid, bulk-elastic-shear and non-surface coverage verdict. source_reviews.independent_solution: Sound vibrations are mechanical disturbances coupled to a medium and capable of producing acoustic propagation. The historical school wording may refer specifically to vibrations that produce an auditory sensation, but the selected definition explicitly states that infrasound and ultrasound are also acoustic phenomena. The seed's 17 and 20000 Hz numbers describe the textbook's approximate hearing convention, not a common absolute perception boundary for every listener and sound-pressure level. In air the acoustic disturbance is longitudinal pressure/density variation with local particle motion; particles do not have to accompany the wave along its full path. The fluid longitudinal description must not exclude ultrasonic shear sound in solids. A correct response must distinguish the audible historical usage from broad acoustics and must not make the old low-frequency number an exact physiological wall.

source_reviews.independent_solution: For a small disturbance, the acoustic speed relative to the gas satisfies v^2=(partial p/partial rho)_s. In an ideal gas with approximately constant heat-capacity ratio gamma, an adiabatic change gives v^2=gamma*p/rho. Substituting p=rho*R_s*T gives v^2=gamma*R_s*T. Consequently, at fixed composition and gamma, sound speed increases with absolute temperature. Composition changes the specific gas constant and heat capacities; humidity can matter by changing the composition. At fixed temperature and composition, pressure and density scale together, so pressure alone does not change this ideal-model speed. Wind alters propagation relative to the ground, not this intrinsic speed relative to the air. In the ordinary small-amplitude approximately nondispersive regime, changing loudness or pure-tone frequency does not directly set that speed.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Loudness is a perceptual property. For comparable sound at the same listener's ear under fixed frequency, medium and other listening conditions, greater pressure amplitude gives greater intensity and generally greater perceived loudness. For an ordinary linear traveling wave, I=p_rms^2/(rho*v), so the physical intensity scales with squared pressure amplitude. This does not make subjective loudness equal to intensity or universally proportional to amplitude squared. Hearing sensitivity, frequency, duration, listener and environment also matter. For audible pure tones, pitch mainly follows vibration frequency: higher frequency normally means higher pitch. Increasing the amplitude of the same tone usually makes it louder rather than higher in pitch. Complex sounds require periodicity and spectral context and may have no single definite pitch.
